title: Civic association and bridging contact are emerging as a political infrastructure between social decline, belonging, and populist backlash
source_unit: USC Schaeffer Center, The Schaeffer Index: Initial Findings from a 20-Country Study of Populism
geography: 20 countries: United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Germany, United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Austria, Portugal, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa

observations.period: July 2025 survey; social, political, and economic decline across 20 countries

denominator.unit: approximately adults across nationally representative samples in 20 countries

values_loss.unit: percent globally agreeing that society has lost touch with the values that built the nation

political_system.value: a majority in every surveyed country agreed that the political system was broken; more than three-quarters did so in Spain, Argentina, France, South Africa, and the United States

financial_disappointment.value: roughly half in every country felt poorer than expected; 61% in the United States and 56% in the United Kingdom were financially disappointed

backlash_route.value: economic and institutional disappointment creates a broad context in which nostalgia and political backlash can become meaningful, but does not establish a single cause

observations.method: First annual round of the Schaeffer Index survey, collected in July 2025 across nationally representative samples in 20 countries; USC public summary reports descriptive cross-country findings.
observations.uncertainty: The public article does not provide full weighting, country sample sizes, question wording for every measure, or the forthcoming longitudinal/statistical model; results are not causal estimates.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 20 countries with different economic conditions, political systems, civic institutions, social networks, and exposure to populist-nationalist parties.
observations.counterinterpretation: Nostalgia, distrust, and financial disappointment may be correlated expressions of broader conditions rather than a pathway from economic decline to populism.

no_group_participation.unit: percent saying they do not participate in any civic association, group, or club

meaningful_frequency.unit: percent participating in an activity with meaningful frequency across the 20 countries

group_mix.value: sports clubs were the most common group at 17%, followed by exercise classes and religious groups at 13% each; political parties were least common at 4%

civic_infrastructure.value: weak or uneven associational participation may reduce routine opportunities to build trust, shared identity, and practical political voice

observations.method: Cross-sectional survey asking about participation in sports, unions, parties, cultural groups, volunteering, professional organizations, and other associations.
observations.uncertainty: Participation frequency is self-reported and the article does not establish whether low participation reflects cost, time, exclusion, lack of supply, distrust, or preference; no causal effect is estimated.
observations.subgroup: People with different social time, income, care duties, transportation, access to organizations, and local civic infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal group participation is not the whole of social life; family, informal mutual aid, online groups, and issue-specific action may be meaningful but not captured by the measure.

observations.period: July 2025 survey; friendship, participation, and bridging contact

few_close_friends.unit: percent reporting three close friends or fewer

bridging_contact.value: 63% of group participants reported meeting people different from them daily or weekly, compared with 46% of nonparticipants

belonging_association.value: participants in every surveyed country were more likely to report higher community belonging

mechanism.value: association can create repeated contact across lines of difference, which may connect social belonging to political tolerance and institutional confidence

observations.method: Cross-sectional survey comparison of friendship, group participation, community belonging, and contact across racial, class, religious, social, and political difference.
observations.uncertainty: The observed associations do not show whether participation creates bridging contact or whether people with more networks select into groups; social-group quality and power relations are not fully measured.
observations.subgroup: People with different numbers of close friends, group membership, and exposure to diverse social settings.
observations.counterinterpretation: Contact across difference can produce conflict or reinforce boundaries if groups are unequal, polarized, or organized around exclusion; diversity of contact is not automatically deliberative quality.

observations.period: July 2025 survey; political diversity within groups and populist-nationalist support

populist_support.unit: percent of all survey participants reporting a vote for populist-nationalist parties

homogeneous_religious_group.unit: percent reporting populist-nationalist voting among participants in very politically homogeneous religious organizations

diverse_religious_group.unit: percent reporting populist-nationalist voting among participants in very politically diverse religious organizations

political_diversity_route.value: the political diversity of groups may matter more than membership alone for whether association creates bridging rather than insulated identity

observations.method: Survey comparison using reported participation and organization-level political homogeneity/diversity, with populist-nationalist party classification based on Stanford’s Votes for Populists dataset and Cas Mudde’s definition.
observations.uncertainty: These are descriptive associations; party support, group composition, self-selection, country context, and organization type may confound the relationship, and classification is contestable.
observations.subgroup: Participants in religious and other organizations with different levels of political diversity, plus supporters and non-supporters of populist-nationalist parties.
observations.counterinterpretation: Politically diverse groups may attract people who already hold more pluralist views; group diversity could be an outcome of prior attitudes rather than their cause.

related_sources.claim: Official USC Schaeffer public summary of the initial 20-country Schaeffer Index findings and survey methodology.
USC Center for Civic Society institutional context for the index’s civic-infrastructure and political-attitudes research program.

boundary: This record adds a comparative political-culture route linking decline perceptions, financial disappointment, civic association, friendship, bridging contact, political diversity, belonging, and populist-nationalist support. It uses an initial 2025 survey round summarized in a 2026 public article, not respondent-level atlas ingestion, causal evidence, longitudinal results, election forecasts, or proof that civic groups reduce populism.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official USC Schaeffer article reviewed for field date, approximately 32,000-adult/20-country sample, decline and trust findings, group participation, friendship, bridging contact, populist-nationalist comparisons, party classification, and planned future modeling.
